title: How does a hummingbird hover in mid-air?
hook: It beats its wings dozens of times a second and gets lift even on the way back up.
summary: A hummingbird beats its wings dozens of times a second and makes lift on both the down-stroke and the up-stroke; at night it can drop into torpor to save energy.
cardText: Beating its wings dozens of times a second, a hummingbird makes lift as each wing sweeps down and again as it comes back up. No other bird can hold still in the air for so long.

cardBlocks.text: A helicopter can hold still in the air because its rotor never stops pushing air downwards. A hummingbird solves the same problem with its wings, beating them extremely fast: 70 to 80 times a second in the smallest species. It is the only bird that can hover like this for long, and it can fly backwards too.

The secret is making the return stroke count. Measurements of rufous hummingbirds in 2005 showed that the down-stroke provides 75% of the lift and the up-stroke 25%: on the way up the wing flips over and keeps working, in a style of flight that resembles an insect’s. All that effort comes at a price. To avoid starving overnight, a hummingbird can slip into torpor, a very deep sleep-like state in which its metabolism drops to a minimum and its body cools down.
Hummingbirds hover by beating their wings very fast and making lift on both strokes; at night they save energy in torpor.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Same beat for hovering and cruising

A hummingbird beats its wings at the same rate whether it is hovering or flying forwards. The rate differs between species and even between the sexes: in Calliphlox amethystina, one of the smallest species, the male beats its wings about 80 times a second and the larger female about 60.

A later study tracked the air around the wings of hovering hummingbirds. Lift does not vanish when the wing changes direction: the wing’s rotation between down-stroke and up-stroke keeps the airflow attached, so lift is produced almost continuously through the wingbeat, something not previously known in any vertebrate.

A ruby-throated hummingbird’s heart beats about 225 times a minute at rest and more than 1,200 times a minute in flight. That is why torpor matters so much: it can cut the resting metabolic rate to a tenth. It is not hibernation, which lasts a long time; a hummingbird can go into torpor on any night of the year when cold and lack of food demand it.
Hummingbirds live only in the Americas, and Brazil and Ecuador together hold about half of all known species. According to WikiAves, 90 species of the family live in Brazil.
